_description: Maps research goals to prioritized record type sequences. Order matters — first records are highest priority for that goal.

strategies.description: Finding parents requires records that explicitly name them. Birth records and census returns (especially 1880+) are the most direct sources.
Census records list household members. Probate records and obituaries often enumerate children. Church baptism records name parents.
Marriage records are the primary source. Census records show household composition. Death records and obituaries often name spouses.
Census records listing entire households are the best starting point. Probate records may name all heirs. Obituaries often list surviving siblings.
Confirming identity requires multiple independent sources placing the same person in the same time and place. Cross-reference census, vital records, and directory listings.
General exploration starts with the most information-rich records (census, vital records) and expands outward to fill gaps.
Immigration and naturalization records may name the town of origin. Census records (1900+) ask year of immigration. Church records may connect to a home parish.
Start with service records and pension files. Newspaper coverage of veterans is common. Census records (1910, 1930, 1940) include veteran status questions.
